stem:
An ED liaison clinician sees a 41-year-old after a self-inflicted forearm wound. Medical assessment and wound care are under way. He drank earlier; his blood alcohol concentration is 0.09 g/100 mL. He is alert, attentive, gives a coherent account and denies current suicidal intent. He wants to discuss what happened. A colleague suggests postponing all mental-health assessment until the result is below 0.05 g/100 mL.

What is the best response?

options.label: A
options.text: Defer assessment until a repeat result is below the proposed threshold
options.explanation: A fixed alcohol concentration does not establish whether someone can participate. Clinical assessment of engagement and cognition should determine what can be done now.

options.label: B
options.text: Begin assessment now and reassess as the alcohol effects resolve
options.explanation: He can engage, so an initial psychosocial assessment should begin alongside medical care. Alcohol can affect the account and mental state, making continued observation and reassessment important.

options.label: C
options.text: Base disposition on his current denial of suicidal intent
options.explanation: A denial of intent alone does not establish a safe disposition, especially after recent self-harm and alcohol use. A fuller assessment and plan are needed.

options.label: D
options.text: Complete wound care before beginning any psychosocial assessment
options.explanation: Psychosocial assessment need not wait until medical treatment is finished when the person can participate. The two can proceed together.

options.label: E
options.text: Arrange community mental-health follow-up without an ED assessment
options.explanation: Referral without assessment skips the risk assessment he needs today; he can engage now, and any follow-up should be planned from that assessment.

context: After self-harm, start psychosocial assessment as early as the person can participate; use clinical reassessment rather than a fixed alcohol threshold.
